sections.title: From tokens to megawatts
ps: ByteDance is two businesses that meet in the data centre. Its consumer apps — Douyin, TikTok, the Doubao assistant — generate the demand: video to transcode, feeds to rank, questions to answer. Volcano Engine, its cloud, sells the same machinery to others, above all as {{MaaS}}: its own Doubao-Seed models and third-party models served through an API and billed per {{token}}.

A token is a word or a piece of one. Every token a model reads or writes is arithmetic on an {{AI accelerator}}, and arithmetic is electricity. Volcano Engine's president said in June 2026 that Doubao was processing 180 trillion tokens a day. The chain from that number to a power order runs: more tokens → more accelerator-hours of {{inference}} → more accelerators → more racks → more megawatts of {{critical IT load}} → more transformers, rectifiers, batteries and switchgear.

Two things break the chain's simplicity. The energy per token keeps falling as chips and models improve, so token growth overstates power growth. And the accelerators do not all sit in ByteDance's own buildings, or even in China: some capacity is leased from landlords and some is rented abroad. Where a given megawatt sits decides who buys its power equipment — the subject of most of this guide.

sections.title: How a token is priced, and what the price structure teaches
sections.intro: List prices on Volcano Engine's model platform (RMB per million tokens, online inference, page of 24 September 2026). The structure of the price is a map of where the accelerator's time goes.

sections.title: Why output costs three to five times input
ps: **Input is read in parallel.** When a prompt arrives, the model processes all its tokens together in one pass — the accelerator's arithmetic units are kept busy, and the cost per token is low.

**Output is written one token at a time.** Each new token needs a full pass through the model's weights, and the next cannot start until the last is finished. That pass is limited by how fast weights can be read from memory, not by arithmetic, so each output token occupies the accelerator far longer. Hence output prices three to five times the input price in the table.

**A cache hit skips work already done.** If a prompt repeats a prefix the platform has already processed, it can reuse the stored intermediate state instead of recomputing it — so the price falls to between a quarter and a thirtieth of the input price, and the platform charges separately for holding that state in memory (0.017 RMB per million tokens per hour).

**Why a power seller cares.** Output-heavy, long-context workloads are the ones that fill racks with memory-rich accelerators and keep them busy around the clock; that is the load profile the power chain is being sized for.

sections.title: Racks × density = megawatts
ps: A data centre's size is usually quoted in megawatts of {{critical IT load}}, but a permit or a tender often lists racks. The conversion is multiplication: racks × kilowatts per rack. One of ByteDance's campuses, the second phase of the Taihang computing centre in Datong, was approved as 15,604 racks at 12 kW each — 15,604 × 12 kW ≈ 187 MW, which is the figure a landlord's filing gives for it.

Twelve kilowatts is a conventional rack. An AI {{supernode}} draws 100 to 350 kW. The same 187 MW of IT load would fill about 4,700 racks at 40 kW, about 1,440 at 130 kW, or about 535 at 350 kW. The power does not shrink when the racks do; it concentrates. A hall that once spread 187 MW over thousands of rows now has to deliver it to a few hundred cabinets, which is what drives the move to liquid cooling and higher distribution voltages.

Read in reverse, the arithmetic is a check on any claim. A campus described by rack count and density can be converted to megawatts and compared with the substation behind it; if the two disagree by a factor, one of the numbers describes something else.

sections.title: Reading an 'HVDC share' and an '800 V pilot'
ps: In a Chinese hyperscale fleet, 'HVDC penetration' means the share of IT load fed by {{240 VDC}} or 336 V DC systems rather than by AC {{UPS}} units. A higher share means fewer conversions and a DC bus the batteries sit on directly. It is a fleet average, so it moves slowly: every hall already built keeps the chain it was built with.

An '800 V pilot' is a different kind of step. At {{800 VDC}} the rack is fed at a voltage high enough for 100-kilowatt-plus racks without enormous currents, and the source can be a {{transformer-rectifier unit}} or an {{SST}}. A 'building-level, tens-of-megawatts' pilot would mean one hall fed that way — a test of the whole chain, from the source through DC protection to the racks, not a fleet change.

What the record holds for ByteDance is thinner than the talk. The only figures for either — HVDC at 30 to 40 percent and a tens-of-MW 800 V pilot — trace to one unattributed exhibition post in January 2026; the same site wrote a week later that the 800 V work was 'still out to tender'. In September 2026 a mainstream financial paper confirmed only that ByteDance had 'first introduced' an 800 V HVDC scheme, with no share, size or supplier. No supplier's filing announces a ByteDance 800 V or SST award.

The distinction to hold is between a tender and an award. A tender is the buyer asking for bids; an award names who won, and in China a listed supplier's winning of a material order usually surfaces in its own filings. Until an award is public, an 800 V programme at ByteDance is a signal of intent.

sections.title: Why an SST's transformer is the hard part
ps: **The component.** An {{SST}} replaces the 50 Hz iron transformer with power cells that switch at thousands of hertz, each with a small {{medium-frequency transformer}} to provide {{galvanic isolation}}. Its core shrinks roughly in proportion to the frequency.

**The difficulty.** The winding must still withstand the full medium-voltage insulation stress, now in a much smaller volume, under the very fast voltage edges that {{SiC}} transistors produce. Insulation, heat and partial discharge — tiny sparks inside the insulation that slowly destroy it — all get harder as the part shrinks.

**Why it matters for reading claims.** When a supplier says its SST's 'core medium-voltage high-frequency transformer' is at sample testing, it is saying the one part that makes the device an SST is not yet qualified. That is why an SST award is a meaningful event and a tender is not.

sections.title: Reading three capex numbers that disagree
ps: **The numbers.** For ByteDance's 2026 {{capex}} the press has reported a preliminary RMB 160 billion (December 2025), more than RMB 200 billion (May 2026) and up to US$70 billion under discussion (May 2026). Low to high, the spread is about three times. ByteDance has confirmed none of them.

**Why they can all be true.** A budget, a revised budget and a ceiling under discussion are different things. Scope differs too: AI infrastructure or all capex; China or worldwide; owned equipment only, or including the leases and rented GPUs that are really operating expense. And a figure in dollars from one date and a figure in yuan from another are not the same measurement.

**How to use them.** Quote the range, name the scope of each, and anchor on what is independently dated — for a private company, lenders' and landlords' filings often say more than leaks do. Never average leaks into a 'consensus'.

sections.title: Chips, borders and where the buildings go
ps: **The rule.** US {{export controls}} restrict which advanced accelerators may be sold to Chinese companies and where they may run. The result is a split compute map.

**The split.** Inside China, capacity runs on the imported chips that can still be had and on domestic accelerators — which, chip for chip, generally draw more power for the same work. Outside China, capacity is leased or rented where the newest GPUs can legally run: campuses in Southeast Asia, Europe and Latin America, and GPU clouds that own the chips themselves.

**The consequence for power equipment.** Only the first half of that map buys Chinese power equipment through Chinese procurement. The overseas half buys it — if at all — through local landlords and their own supply chains, and rented GPUs buy none. A seller in China is selling into the domestic half, where the chip mix sets the rack power envelope.

sections.title: Where it fails
ps: **Quoting the 30–40% HVDC share or the tens-of-MW 800 V pilot as fact.** Neither traces to a primary source.
**Treating a tender as an award.** No 800 V or SST award to a named supplier is public.
**Reading silence as absence.** Chinese suppliers often anonymise large internet customers; a filing that does not name ByteDance proves nothing either way.
**Picking one capex number.** Three leaks with different scopes bracket a range; none is confirmed.
**Selling to only one party in a leased hall.** The landlord places the order; the tenant's list decides who may win it.
**Counting overseas and rented capacity as power-equipment demand in China.** Rented GPUs buy no transformers, and overseas halls buy through their owners.

cards.q: Why is an output token priced several times higher than an input token?
cards.a: Input tokens are processed together in one parallel pass; output tokens are generated one at a time, each needing a full pass through the model's weights, so each occupies the accelerator far longer.

cards.q: What is a cache hit in model pricing, and why is it cheaper?
cards.a: Reuse of the stored intermediate state for a prompt prefix the platform has already processed, so the work is not repeated; the platform charges less per token and a separate fee for holding the state in memory.

cards.q: Trace a rise in daily tokens to a power-equipment order.
cards.a: More tokens → more accelerator-hours → more accelerators → more racks → more megawatts of IT load → more transformers, rectifiers, UPS, switchgear and distribution — offset by falling energy per token.

cards.q: Name the three doors through which a hyperscaler's power equipment is bought.
cards.a: Its own campuses (it orders directly and writes the spec); leased halls (the landlord orders, often from the tenant's qualified list); rented capacity (the owner buys; the tenant buys no equipment).

cards.q: A campus has 15,600 racks at 12 kW. What is its IT load, and how many 350 kW racks carry the same?
cards.a: About 187 MW; about 535 racks. The power is unchanged — it is concentrated into far fewer cabinets.

cards.q: What does 'HVDC penetration' measure in a Chinese data-centre fleet?
cards.a: The share of IT load fed by 240 or 336 V DC systems instead of AC UPS; a fleet average that moves slowly because built halls keep their chains.

cards.q: What is the difference between a tender and an award?
cards.a: A tender asks for bids; an award names the winner. Only an award — usually visible in a listed supplier's filings — shows that business exists.

cards.q: Why is the medium-frequency transformer the hardest part of an SST?
cards.a: It must hold full medium-voltage insulation in a much smaller volume under the fast voltage edges of SiC switching, where heat and partial discharge are hardest to control.

cards.q: Why can three reported capex figures differ threefold without any being false?
cards.a: They measure different things — budget, revised budget, ceiling; AI or total; China or global; owned assets or including leases and rentals — at different dates and in different currencies.

cards.q: Why do rented overseas GPUs not show up in capex?
cards.a: The renter pays the owner as operating expense; the chips, the building and its power equipment are the owner's assets.

cards.q: Why is a tenant's self-build a risk for its wholesale landlord?
cards.a: The tenant moves its growth into buildings it owns, and a landlord that depends on one tenant faces the renewal with little leverage.
